motivation: in recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered by the discovery of the laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure in solutions
oneLiner: First chemistry Nobel: laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure in solutions.

deepDive.scope: Van 't Hoff won the inaugural Nobel Prize in Chemistry for founding physical chemistry through two linked achievements: the laws of chemical dynamics (reaction rates, chemical equilibrium, and the temperature dependence of equilibrium captured in the van 't Hoff equation) and the law of osmotic pressure in dilute solutions. His 1884 book 'Etudes de dynamique chimique' (Studies in Chemical Dynamics) established quantitative reaction kinetics and equilibrium, while his 1886 work showed that dissolved solutes obey a gas-like law, p = cRT.
deepDive.history: Working in the late 19th century alongside Arrhenius and Ostwald, van 't Hoff helped create physical chemistry as a discipline distinct from classical descriptive chemistry. Earlier he had also proposed (1874) the tetrahedral carbon atom, founding stereochemistry, though the Nobel honored his thermodynamic and kinetic work specifically.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Van 't Hoff treated dissolved molecules as analogous to gas molecules. He showed that the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution equals the pressure the solute would exert as an ideal gas occupying the same volume: pi = cRT, where c is molar concentration, R the gas constant, and T absolute temperature. This unified solution behavior with the kinetic theory of gases.

In chemical dynamics he formalized how reaction rate depends on concentration and how equilibrium constants shift with temperature. The van 't Hoff equation, d(ln K)/dT = DeltaH/(RT^2), relates the temperature dependence of an equilibrium constant to the reaction enthalpy, providing a thermodynamic bridge between heat and chemical change.

He distinguished forward and reverse reactions reaching a dynamic equilibrium where rates balance, and connected equilibrium constants to free energy. This gave chemists predictive, quantitative tools rather than purely empirical rules.

Notably, anomalies in osmotic pressure for salts (which gave pressures too high by a factor i) hinted that solutes could split into multiple particles, a clue that fed directly into Arrhenius's dissociation theory honored two years later.
concepts: Osmotic pressure: the pressure needed to stop solvent flowing into a solution through a semipermeable membrane, proportional to solute concentration.
Chemical equilibrium: a dynamic state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
van 't Hoff equation: relates how an equilibrium constant changes with temperature to the reaction enthalpy.

jargon.definition: The 'pull' a solution exerts on pure solvent across a membrane; more dissolved particles means stronger pull.
The study of how fast reactions go and where they settle (equilibrium).
A number i counting how many particles one dissolved formula unit becomes in solution.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Van 't Hoff's laws gave chemistry a rigorous thermodynamic and kinetic foundation, enabling prediction of reaction direction, yield, and rate. Osmotic theory underpins biology (cell turgor, dialysis) and the van 't Hoff equation remains standard in every physical chemistry course.

learnMore.note: His own account of osmotic theory.

motivation: in recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered by his work on sugar and purine syntheses
oneLiner: Synthesis and stereochemistry of sugars and purines; founded biomolecular organic chemistry.

deepDive.scope: Emil Fischer won for elucidating and synthesizing two central classes of biological molecules: sugars (carbohydrates) and purines (the base skeleton of caffeine, uric acid, and the nucleic-acid bases adenine and guanine). He determined the stereochemical configurations of the hexose sugars and devised total syntheses of glucose, fructose, and mannose, and synthesized the parent purine and many derivatives.
deepDive.history: In the 1880s-1890s the three-dimensional structure of molecules was newly understood (after van 't Hoff). Fischer applied this to the dauntingly complex sugar molecules, each with multiple stereocenters, and to the purine family he named. His work bridged synthetic organic chemistry and biochemistry.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Sugars like glucose have several chiral carbons, giving many stereoisomers that are otherwise nearly identical chemically. Fischer used systematic chemical reactions (oxidation, reduction, the Kiliani-Fischer chain extension, and osazone formation with phenylhydrazine) to interrelate the sugars and deduce their relative configurations, work for which he devised the Fischer projection notation still used today.

He assigned configurations to all 16 aldohexoses and synthesized glucose from glycerol, a landmark total synthesis of a natural product. His phenylhydrazine osazone reactions let him distinguish and connect sugars that differ only at certain carbons.

For purines, Fischer recognized that uric acid, xanthine, caffeine, theobromine, and the nucleobases share a common bicyclic skeleton he called 'purine.' He synthesized this core and converted it into dozens of derivatives, proving their structures by synthesis.

This 'lock and key' insight into molecular shape and specificity (which he articulated for enzyme-substrate recognition) anchored the idea that biological function follows precise three-dimensional structure.
concepts: Stereochemistry of sugars: sugars differ by the spatial arrangement of -OH groups around chiral carbons.
Fischer projection: a 2D way of drawing 3D configuration at chiral centers.
Purine skeleton: the fused-ring core shared by caffeine, uric acid, adenine, and guanine.

jargon.definition: Molecules with the same atoms and bonds but different 3D arrangements.
A two-ring nitrogen-containing structure forming the basis of several biomolecules.
A crystalline derivative formed when a sugar reacts with phenylhydrazine, used to identify sugars.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Fischer turned carbohydrate and purine chemistry from confusion into ordered science, founded biochemistry's structural approach, and his lock-and-key concept shaped enzymology. The Fischer projection and his sugar nomenclature remain textbook standards.

flashcards.front: What classes of molecules did Emil Fischer's Nobel work cover?
flashcards.back: Sugars (carbohydrates) and purines.

flashcards.front: What notation did Fischer invent for sugar stereochemistry?
flashcards.back: The Fischer projection.

flashcards.back: Adenine and guanine (also caffeine, uric acid).

motivation: in recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered to the advancement of chemistry by his electrolytic theory of dissociation
oneLiner: Electrolytic theory of dissociation: salts split into mobile ions in solution.

deepDive.scope: Arrhenius won for his theory of electrolytic dissociation, the idea (advanced in his 1884 doctoral thesis and developed through 1887) that electrolytes such as salts, acids, and bases spontaneously split into electrically charged ions when dissolved in water, even without an applied current. This explained electrical conductivity of solutions and reframed acids and bases in terms of H+ and OH- ions.
deepDive.history: Arrhenius's dissertation was received coolly (a low passing grade) because the notion of free charged ions seemed radical. Support from van 't Hoff and Ostwald helped vindicate it; together the three are considered founders of physical chemistry. The anomalous van 't Hoff factor i for salts had foreshadowed dissociation.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Arrhenius proposed that in solution a compound like NaCl exists not as intact molecules but as separated Na+ and Cl- ions. These mobile charges carry current, explaining why solutions conduct electricity, with conductivity rising as dilution increases the fraction dissociated.

The theory explained colligative anomalies: a salt that splits into two ions depresses freezing point and raises osmotic pressure roughly twice as much as a non-dissociating solute of the same molarity, matching van 't Hoff's factor i.

It also recast acid-base chemistry: an acid is a substance that releases H+ ions in water, a base one that releases OH-, and neutralization is simply H+ + OH- forming water. Strong acids dissociate nearly completely; weak ones only partially, defined by a dissociation constant.

This ionic picture connected chemistry to electricity and thermodynamics, underpinning electrochemistry, pH, and reaction-rate theory (Arrhenius later gave the famous activation-energy rate equation, though the Nobel cited dissociation).
concepts: Electrolytic dissociation: dissolved electrolytes separate into free ions.
Acid/base in Arrhenius terms: acids give H+, bases give OH- in water.
Degree of dissociation: the fraction of dissolved molecules that have split into ions, rising with dilution.

jargon.definition: A substance whose water solution conducts electricity because it forms ions.
An atom or molecule carrying a net electric charge.
The splitting of a compound into smaller charged pieces in solution.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Arrhenius's ion theory is foundational to all of electrochemistry, acid-base chemistry, pH, biological ion transport, and analytical chemistry. The concept that solutions teem with free ions is now so basic it is taught in introductory courses.

flashcards.front: What is Arrhenius's electrolytic theory of dissociation?
flashcards.back: Electrolytes split into free ions when dissolved in water.

flashcards.front: How did Arrhenius define an acid?
flashcards.back: A substance that releases H+ ions in water.

flashcards.front: Why do salt solutions conduct electricity?
flashcards.back: Mobile dissociated ions carry the current.

motivation: in recognition of his services in the discovery of the inert gaseous elements in air, and his determination of their place in the periodic system
oneLiner: Discovered the noble gases and placed them in a new group of the periodic table.

deepDive.scope: Ramsay won for discovering the inert (noble) gases, argon, neon, krypton, and xenon, and helping identify helium on Earth, and for establishing that they form a new group of the periodic system. Working with Lord Rayleigh he isolated argon (1894), then over 1895-1898 the others.
deepDive.history: Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen from air was slightly denser than nitrogen made chemically, hinting at an unknown heavier component. Ramsay removed oxygen and nitrogen from air and found a chemically unreactive residue, argon, an entirely new kind of element with no known reactions.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Ramsay isolated the gases by fractional distillation of liquefied air and by chemically stripping away reactive components, leaving residues that refused to combine with anything. Their inertness and atomic spectra (bright characteristic emission lines) confirmed them as new elements.

The puzzle was where they fit in Mendeleev's periodic table. Their zero valence and monatomic, unreactive character placed them in a new vertical group (group 0/18) between the halogens and the alkali metals, completing each period.

This required and validated an extension of the periodic law: a whole family of elements with closed, stable electron arrangements (later understood as filled electron shells) that explains their reluctance to react.

Ramsay also identified terrestrial helium (previously seen only in the Sun's spectrum) emanating from uranium minerals, linking the noble gases to radioactivity.
concepts: Noble gases: chemically inert elements forming group 18 of the periodic table.
Fractional distillation of air: separating gases by their different boiling points.
Periodic completeness: the inert gases fill the gap between halogens and alkali metals.

jargon.definition: A gas that essentially does not undergo chemical reactions.
The unique set of light wavelengths an element emits, used as a fingerprint.
Existing as single, unbonded atoms rather than molecules.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Discovering an entire new column of the periodic table confirmed and extended the periodic law and later helped explain chemical bonding through filled electron shells. Noble gases are now vital in lighting, cryogenics, lasers, and inert atmospheres.

flashcards.front: Which gases did Ramsay discover?
flashcards.back: Argon, neon, krypton, xenon (and isolated terrestrial helium).

flashcards.front: Where did the noble gases fit in the periodic table?
flashcards.back: A new group (group 0/18) between halogens and alkali metals.

flashcards.front: What property defines the noble gases?
flashcards.back: Chemical inertness from stable, filled electron shells.

laureates: Johann Friedrich Wilhelm Adolf von Baeyer
motivation: in recognition of his services in the advancement of organic chemistry and the chemical industry, through his work on organic dyes and hydroaromatic compounds
oneLiner: Synthesized indigo and advanced organic dye and hydroaromatic chemistry.

deepDive.scope: Baeyer won for advancing organic chemistry and industry through his work on organic dyes, especially the synthesis and structure determination of indigo, and on hydroaromatic compounds. He achieved the laboratory synthesis of indigo and elucidated its structure, and contributed the strain theory of carbon rings.
deepDive.history: Natural indigo was a major dye commodity; Baeyer's structural and synthetic work (from the 1870s-1880s) opened the path to synthetic indigo, which BASF later commercialized, transforming the dye industry and the global indigo trade.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Baeyer determined the chemical structure of indigo and developed synthetic routes to it, demonstrating that a complex natural colorant could be built from simpler aromatic precursors. This proved the power of structural organic chemistry to reproduce and improve on nature.

His study of hydroaromatic compounds (partially saturated ring systems) and of polyacetylenes led to his strain theory, which related the stability of carbocyclic rings to the deviation of their bond angles from the ideal tetrahedral angle, explaining why five- and six-membered rings form most readily.

He also studied phthalein and fluorescein dyes, connecting molecular structure to color, the basis of chromophore theory.

Together this work tied molecular architecture to both physical properties (color) and reactivity/stability (ring strain), guiding synthetic strategy.
concepts: Dye synthesis: building colored molecules (chromophores) by organic synthesis.
Baeyer strain theory: ring stability depends on how much bond angles deviate from ideal.
Structure determination: deducing a molecule's connectivity by chemical reactions.

jargon.definition: The part of a molecule responsible for its color.
A ring compound related to aromatics but with some added hydrogens (partially saturated).
Extra energy in a ring when its bond angles are forced away from ideal.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Synthetic indigo revolutionized the dye industry and showcased industrial organic synthesis. Baeyer's strain theory remains central to understanding ring chemistry and conformational analysis.

flashcards.front: What famous dye did Baeyer synthesize and structurally elucidate?
flashcards.back: Indigo.

flashcards.front: What does Baeyer strain theory relate?
flashcards.back: Ring stability to deviation of bond angles from the ideal tetrahedral angle.

motivation: in recognition of the great services rendered by him in his investigation and isolation of the element fluorine, and for the adoption in the service of science of the electric furnace called after him
oneLiner: Isolated fluorine by electrolysis and developed the high-temperature electric furnace.

deepDive.scope: Moissan won for isolating elemental fluorine, the most reactive element, which had defeated chemists for decades, and for developing the Moissan electric arc furnace for high-temperature chemistry. He first isolated fluorine in 1886 by low-temperature electrolysis of anhydrous hydrogen fluoride.
deepDive.history: Fluorine's extreme reactivity had injured or killed several earlier experimenters and resisted all isolation attempts. Moissan succeeded where others failed, then turned to the electric furnace to reach temperatures (around 3500 C) enabling new high-temperature syntheses, including artificial gemstone attempts and metal carbides.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Free fluorine cannot be obtained by ordinary chemical oxidation because no common oxidizer is strong enough, so Moissan used electrolysis. He electrolyzed a solution of potassium hydrogen fluoride in anhydrous liquid hydrogen fluoride at low temperature (about -50 C) in a platinum apparatus, liberating pale-yellow fluorine gas at the anode.

The low temperature and anhydrous conditions were essential: water would react instantly, and the apparatus had to resist fluorine's corrosiveness, hence platinum-iridium and fluorspar components.

His electric furnace passed a powerful arc between carbon electrodes to reach extreme temperatures, letting him vaporize and recombine refractory materials, prepare carbides (e.g., calcium carbide, silicon carbide) and study refractory metals.

This married electrochemistry and high-temperature inorganic chemistry, expanding the range of conditions chemists could exploit.
concepts: Electrolytic isolation: using electric current to drive a non-spontaneous redox separation.
Reactivity of fluorine: it is the strongest common oxidizer, so it must be made electrolytically.
Electric arc furnace: a device reaching thousands of degrees for refractory chemistry.

jargon.definition: Using electricity to force a chemical reaction that won't happen on its own.
Containing no water.
Able to withstand very high temperatures without melting or decomposing.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Isolating fluorine completed the halogen family experimentally and opened fluorine chemistry (now vital for refrigerants, Teflon, pharmaceuticals, uranium enrichment). The electric furnace enabled industrial production of carbides and abrasives.

flashcards.front: How did Moissan isolate fluorine?
flashcards.back: Low-temperature electrolysis of anhydrous HF containing potassium hydrogen fluoride.

flashcards.front: What apparatus is named after Moissan?
flashcards.back: The Moissan electric (arc) furnace.

motivation: for his biochemical researches and his discovery of cell-free fermentation
oneLiner: Showed fermentation is driven by enzymes (zymase), not living cells, founding biochemistry.

deepDive.scope: Buchner won for discovering cell-free fermentation: in 1897 he showed that a cell-free extract pressed from yeast could ferment sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, proving that fermentation is caused by soluble enzymes (which he attributed to a substance he called 'zymase') rather than requiring intact living cells.
deepDive.history: A long debate (Pasteur vs. Liebig) pitted 'vitalist' views, that fermentation needed living cells, against chemical views. Buchner's accidental discovery, while preserving yeast juice with sugar, settled it decisively in favor of chemistry: enzymes do the work.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Buchner ground yeast with sand and pressed out a cell-free juice containing no living cells. When he added sugar (to preserve the extract), it bubbled, producing alcohol and CO2, fermentation without any organism.

This demonstrated that the catalytic agents of fermentation are molecules, enzymes, that function outside the cell. He named the active principle zymase; later work showed fermentation is actually a cascade of many enzymes.

The result generalized: biological transformations are chemical reactions catalyzed by specific protein enzymes, which can be studied in vitro. This founded modern biochemistry and enzymology.

It connected to Fischer's lock-and-key enzyme specificity and set the stage for the 1929 Harden/Euler-Chelpin Nobel on the detailed enzymatic steps of sugar fermentation.
concepts: Cell-free fermentation: sugar can be fermented by extracts lacking living cells.
Enzyme catalysis: biological reactions are sped by specific protein catalysts.
Mechanism over vitalism: life's chemistry obeys ordinary chemical principles.

jargon.definition: The breakdown of sugar into alcohol and CO2 (or other products) by enzymes.
A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds a specific reaction.
Buchner's name for the soluble fermenting agent of yeast (now known to be many enzymes).

deepDive.whyItMatters: Buchner's experiment launched biochemistry by showing life's reactions can be reproduced in a test tube with enzymes, enabling the entire field of metabolic and enzyme research.

flashcards.front: What did Buchner discover about fermentation?
flashcards.back: It can occur cell-free, driven by enzymes (zymase), not living cells.

flashcards.front: Why is Buchner's work foundational?
flashcards.back: It founded biochemistry by showing biological reactions are enzyme-catalyzed chemistry.

motivation: for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements, and the chemistry of radioactive substances
oneLiner: Showed radioactivity is atomic disintegration, transmuting one element into another.

deepDive.scope: Rutherford won for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements and the chemistry of radioactive substances. With Frederick Soddy he formulated (around 1902-1903) the disintegration theory of radioactivity: radioactive atoms spontaneously transform into different elements by emitting radiation, a genuine transmutation. He also classified alpha and beta rays and introduced the half-life concept.
deepDive.history: After Becquerel and the Curies discovered radioactivity, its nature was unclear. Rutherford, a physicist, brought rigorous experiments to bear, distinguishing types of radiation and proving radioactive change is atomic, not chemical. (He later, in 1911, discovered the atomic nucleus, but the Nobel honored the transmutation chemistry.)
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Rutherford showed radioactivity involves atoms breaking apart: an unstable atom emits an alpha particle (a helium nucleus) or beta particle (an electron) and becomes an atom of a different element, a daughter product. This was transmutation, long deemed impossible, occurring spontaneously.

He and Soddy traced decay series in which a parent element decays through a chain of radioactive daughters, each with a characteristic rate. Rutherford introduced the half-life: the time for half a sample to decay, a constant for each species, reflecting the probabilistic, first-order nature of decay.

He distinguished alpha rays (positively charged, heavy, stopped by paper), beta rays (light, negative), and later gamma rays, and identified alpha particles as helium nuclei by collecting the gas they form.

Because decay rates are fixed and follow exponential kinetics, radioactivity became a clock (radiometric dating) and a probe of atomic structure, blurring the line between physics and chemistry of the atom.
concepts: Radioactive disintegration: unstable atoms decay into different elements by emitting radiation.
Half-life: the fixed time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.
Alpha and beta particles: the helium-nucleus and electron emissions of radioactive decay.

jargon.definition: The change of one element into another, here by radioactive decay.
A helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons) ejected in some radioactive decays.
A chain of successive radioactive transformations from a parent to a stable end product.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Rutherford established that atoms are not immutable, founding nuclear chemistry and physics. Half-lives enable radiometric dating; the transmutation idea underlies nuclear energy, medicine, and the discovery of isotopes (Soddy, 1921) and artificial radioactivity (Joliot-Curies, 1935).

learnMore.note: On the chemical nature of alpha particles.

flashcards.back: Radioactive atoms spontaneously transmute into different elements by emitting radiation.

flashcards.front: What is a half-life?
flashcards.back: The constant time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.

flashcards.front: What is an alpha particle?
flashcards.back: A helium nucleus emitted in certain radioactive decays.

motivation: in recognition of his work on catalysis and for his investigations into the fundamental principles governing chemical equilibria and rates of reaction
oneLiner: Defined catalysis and the principles of chemical equilibria and reaction rates.

deepDive.scope: Ostwald won for his work on catalysis and on the fundamental principles of chemical equilibrium and reaction rates. He gave catalysis its modern definition, a catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed and without changing the equilibrium position, and was a principal founder of physical chemistry alongside van 't Hoff and Arrhenius.
deepDive.history: Ostwald systematized physical chemistry, founded its first major journal, and trained many leading chemists. His catalysis concept underpinned industrial chemistry; the Ostwald process for nitric acid (catalytic oxidation of ammonia) is named for him.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Ostwald clarified that a catalyst alters the rate of a reaction by providing an easier pathway but is regenerated, so it is not consumed and does not shift the equilibrium it merely helps the system reach equilibrium faster, speeding forward and reverse reactions equally.

He quantified reaction rates and how they depend on concentration and on catalysts, and applied dissociation theory to define acid and base strengths via their catalytic and conductivity behavior (Ostwald dilution law relates a weak electrolyte's dissociation constant to its concentration).

He distinguished thermodynamic questions (where equilibrium lies) from kinetic ones (how fast it is reached), a crucial conceptual separation, and showed catalysts affect only the latter.

Industrially, this framework enabled the catalytic Ostwald process oxidizing ammonia over platinum gauze to nitric oxide and ultimately nitric acid, linking his theory to large-scale synthesis (and complementing Haber's ammonia).
concepts: Catalysis: speeding a reaction with a substance that is not consumed.
Equilibrium vs kinetics: where a reaction settles versus how fast it gets there.
Ostwald dilution law: relates a weak electrolyte's dissociation to its concentration.

jargon.definition: A substance that accelerates a reaction without being used up.
How fast reactants are converted to products.
The balanced state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Ostwald's catalysis concept is central to virtually all industrial chemistry and biochemistry (enzymes). Separating kinetics from thermodynamics shaped how chemists design and control reactions; the Ostwald process remains key to fertilizer and explosives manufacture.

flashcards.front: How does a catalyst affect equilibrium?
flashcards.back: It does not shift equilibrium; it only speeds the approach to it.

flashcards.front: What industrial process is named for Ostwald?
flashcards.back: The Ostwald process for making nitric acid from ammonia.

motivation: in recognition of his services to organic chemistry and the chemical industry by his pioneer work in the field of alicyclic compounds
oneLiner: Pioneered the chemistry of terpenes and alicyclic compounds from essential oils.

deepDive.scope: Wallach won for pioneering work on alicyclic compounds, especially the terpenes, the fragrant hydrocarbons of essential oils (from turpentine, citrus, mint, camphor). He brought order to a confusing mass of natural oils by systematically separating, characterizing, and interconverting terpenes and establishing their structures.
deepDive.history: Essential oils were industrially important (perfumes, flavors, camphor) but chemically chaotic, many compounds had different names but identical structures. Wallach's careful work from the 1880s onward rationalized the field and supported the fragrance and camphor industries.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Wallach used systematic chemical methods, controlled reactions with reagents like hydrogen chloride, nitrosyl chloride, and bromine to form crystalline derivatives, to distinguish terpenes that were otherwise hard to separate and to prove their structures.

He recognized that many terpenes are built from isoprene-like five-carbon units (foreshadowing the isoprene rule later developed by Ruzicka), and that they form ring (alicyclic) as well as open-chain structures.

By interconverting terpenes and relating them through their reactions, he established a coherent structural framework for the class and clarified relationships among camphor, pinene, limonene, and related molecules.

This structural chemistry of saturated and partially saturated rings (alicyclic compounds) complemented aromatic chemistry and underpinned synthetic fragrance and natural-product chemistry.
concepts: Terpenes: natural hydrocarbons built from isoprene units, abundant in essential oils.
Alicyclic compounds: ring compounds that are not aromatic.
Derivatization: making crystalline derivatives to identify and separate similar compounds.

jargon.definition: A class of fragrant natural hydrocarbons assembled from five-carbon isoprene units.
Describing a ring molecule that is saturated/non-aromatic.
A volatile, fragrant plant oil rich in terpenes.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Wallach founded systematic terpene chemistry, important for perfumes, flavors, camphor, and later for understanding biosynthesis of steroids and rubber. His structural rigor became a model for natural-product chemistry.

flashcards.front: What class of natural compounds did Wallach pioneer?
flashcards.back: Terpenes (alicyclic compounds of essential oils).

flashcards.front: From what repeating unit are terpenes built?
flashcards.back: Five-carbon isoprene units.

motivation: in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element
oneLiner: Discovered radium and polonium, isolated metallic radium, and characterized its chemistry.

deepDive.scope: Marie Curie won her second Nobel (first in physics, 1903) for the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, the isolation of pure metallic radium, and the study of radium's nature and chemical compounds. This 1911 prize honored specifically the chemical achievement of isolating and characterizing a new element.
deepDive.history: Investigating why uranium minerals were more radioactive than uranium alone, Curie (with Pierre Curie) hypothesized undiscovered radioactive elements. In 1898 they announced polonium and radium. Isolating weighable radium required processing tons of pitchblende residues over years of grueling labor.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Curie used radioactivity itself as an analytical tool: she tracked the radioactivity through chemical separations (fractional crystallization) of pitchblende, following which fractions concentrated the activity, a pioneering use of radiotracing to find new elements.

Radium co-precipitated with barium because of their chemical similarity (both group 2). She separated them by repeated fractional crystallization of their chlorides/bromides, exploiting tiny solubility differences, until she obtained pure radium salts and determined radium's atomic weight (about 226).

In 1910, with Andre Debierne, she isolated radium as a metal by electrolysis of molten radium chloride, proving it a genuine new element and placing it in the periodic table below barium.

She characterized radium's emission (its glow, heat output, and gas, radon) and its compounds, establishing radiochemistry as the chemistry of elements identified and tracked by their radioactivity.
concepts: Radiotracing: using radioactivity to follow an element through chemical separations.
Fractional crystallization: separating similar salts by repeated selective crystallization.
Element isolation: proving a new element by obtaining it pure and measuring its atomic weight.

jargon.definition: A uranium-rich ore from which radium and polonium were extracted.
Spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable atomic nuclei.
Separating substances by their slightly different tendencies to crystallize.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Curie's isolation of radium proved radioactivity is an atomic property and created radiochemistry. Radium enabled cancer radiotherapy and research into the atom; her tracer methods became standard. She remains the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences.

learnMore.title: Marie Curie Nobel Lecture
learnMore.note: On radium and the new radioactive substances.

flashcards.front: Which two elements did Marie Curie discover?
flashcards.back: Radium and polonium.

flashcards.front: How was radium separated from chemically similar barium?
flashcards.back: Repeated fractional crystallization of their salts.

flashcards.front: Why is Marie Curie historically unique?
flashcards.back: She won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911).

motivation: Victor Grignard "for the discovery of the so-called Grignard reagent, which in recent years has greatly advanced the progress of organic chemistry"; Paul Sabatier "for his method of hydrogenating organic compounds in the presence of finely disintegrated metals whereby the progress of organic chemistry has been greatly advanced in recent years"
oneLiner: Grignard organometallic reagents and Sabatier's metal-catalyzed hydrogenation.

deepDive.scope: The 1912 prize was shared. Grignard won for discovering organomagnesium halide reagents (Grignard reagents, RMgX), versatile tools for forming carbon-carbon bonds. Sabatier won for his method of catalytically hydrogenating organic compounds using finely divided metals such as nickel, enabling addition of hydrogen to unsaturated molecules.
deepDive.history: Both advances (around 1900-1905) gave synthetic organic chemistry powerful, general new methods. Grignard's reagent came from his doctoral work under Barbier; Sabatier developed gas-phase catalytic hydrogenation that became central to industry (e.g., hardening fats).
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
A Grignard reagent forms when an alkyl or aryl halide reacts with magnesium metal in dry ether, giving RMgX. The carbon bonded to magnesium is strongly nucleophilic (carbanion-like). It attacks electrophilic carbons, notably the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes, ketones, esters, and CO2, forming new C-C bonds and, after workup, alcohols or carboxylic acids. This made building complex carbon skeletons routine.

Sabatier showed that finely divided metals (especially nickel) catalyze the addition of hydrogen gas across carbon-carbon double bonds and other unsaturations. The metal surface dissociates H2 and the unsaturated molecule adsorbs and is hydrogenated, all heterogeneously at the catalyst surface.

Together the prizes recognized two complementary strategies: building molecules up (Grignard C-C bond formation) and selectively saturating them (Sabatier hydrogenation).

Both methods are mild, general, and scalable, and both connect to broader catalysis (Sabatier) and organometallic (Grignard) chemistry that dominate modern synthesis.
concepts: Grignard reagent: an organomagnesium compound that acts as a carbon nucleophile.
Carbonyl addition: Grignard reagents add to C=O to form alcohols.
Catalytic hydrogenation: metals catalyze adding H2 across double bonds.

jargon.definition: A compound containing a carbon-metal bond.
An electron-rich species that attacks electron-poor centers.
Adding hydrogen atoms across a double or triple bond.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Grignard reagents remain among the most used reactions for forming C-C bonds in synthesis. Sabatier hydrogenation is fundamental to petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, and food (margarine), and helped found heterogeneous catalysis.

flashcards.front: What does a Grignard reagent do in synthesis?
flashcards.back: Acts as a carbon nucleophile to form new C-C bonds, e.g., adding to carbonyls to give alcohols.

motivation: in recognition of his work on the linkage of atoms in molecules by which he has thrown new light on earlier investigations and opened up new fields of research especially in inorganic chemistry
oneLiner: Founded coordination chemistry: the 3D structure of metal-ligand complexes.

deepDive.scope: Werner won for his coordination theory of the linkage of atoms in molecules, explaining the structure of metal complexes (coordination compounds). He proposed that metal ions possess a secondary valence (coordination number) through which they bind a defined number of surrounding groups (ligands) arranged in specific three-dimensional geometries.
deepDive.history: Compounds like cobalt-ammine complexes (CoCl3.6NH3 and variants) had baffled chemists, classical valence could not explain why they existed or why isomers occurred. Werner's 1893 coordination theory (he conceived it, the story goes, on waking) resolved this and founded inorganic stereochemistry.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Werner distinguished a metal's primary valence (oxidation state, satisfied by ions) from its secondary valence (coordination number), the fixed number of groups directly bonded to the metal, typically six (octahedral) or four (tetrahedral/square planar).

In a complex like [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, six ammonia ligands occupy the metal's coordination sphere octahedrally, and three chloride ions sit outside as counterions. Replacing ligands changes how many chlorides are ionizable, explaining the series of cobalt-ammine compounds and their conductivities.

Crucially, the octahedral geometry predicts isomers: for [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ there are cis and trans forms, and for certain complexes optical isomers (non-superimposable mirror images). Werner painstakingly prepared and resolved such isomers, even an entirely carbon-free chiral complex, proving the 3D arrangement.

This established that bonding geometry, not just composition, governs inorganic compounds, extending stereochemistry from carbon to metals.
concepts: Coordination number: the number of ligands directly bonded to a metal center.
Ligand: an ion or molecule that donates electrons to bond to a metal.
Geometric and optical isomerism in complexes: spatial arrangements give cis/trans and chiral forms.

jargon.definition: A metal center surrounded by bound ligands.
A molecule or ion attached to a central metal atom.
A geometry with six ligands at the corners of an octahedron around the metal.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Werner's coordination theory founded modern inorganic and organometallic chemistry, essential to catalysis, bioinorganic chemistry (hemoglobin, chlorophyll), materials, and metallurgy. The concepts of ligands and coordination geometry are universal.

flashcards.front: What did Werner's coordination theory introduce?
flashcards.back: The idea of secondary valence (coordination number) and 3D ligand arrangement around metals.

flashcards.front: How did Werner prove complex geometry?
flashcards.back: By preparing and resolving geometric and optical isomers, including a carbon-free chiral complex.

motivation: in recognition of his accurate determinations of the atomic weight of a large number of chemical elements
oneLiner: Made the most accurate atomic-weight determinations, revealing isotopic mass differences in lead.

deepDive.scope: Richards won for exceptionally accurate determinations of the atomic weights of many elements. He redetermined some 25 elements' atomic weights with unprecedented precision, correcting earlier values and notably showing that lead from different radioactive sources has different atomic weights, direct chemical evidence for isotopes.
deepDive.history: Accurate atomic weights were foundational to chemistry and the periodic table, yet many literature values were flawed. Richards developed meticulous techniques to eliminate systematic errors, becoming the first American to win the chemistry Nobel.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Richards identified and eliminated subtle sources of error in classic gravimetric atomic-weight work: contamination, moisture and gases adsorbed on precipitates, occluded solvent, and impure reagents. He invented apparatus (the nephelometer to compare turbidities, and the bottling apparatus to handle hygroscopic samples without air contact) to achieve precision to several significant figures.

By carefully converting weighed amounts of pure compounds (e.g., silver salts) and comparing masses, he refined values for silver, chlorine, and many other elements, putting atomic weights on a reliable footing.

Most strikingly, he found that lead extracted from uranium ores (an endpoint of uranium decay) had a measurably lower atomic weight than ordinary lead, and lead from thorium ores differed too. Since these leads were chemically identical, the mass difference could only mean atoms of the same element can have different masses, isotopes, confirming Soddy's concept chemically.
concepts: Atomic weight determination: measuring the average mass of an element's atoms by precise chemical conversions.
Systematic error control: the heart of high-precision measurement.
Isotopic mass variation: lead from different sources has different atomic weight.

jargon.definition: The average mass of an element's atoms relative to a standard.
Determining amounts by precise weighing of pure compounds.
Atoms of the same element with different masses (different neutron counts).

deepDive.whyItMatters: Reliable atomic weights are bedrock data for all of chemistry. Richards's discovery that lead's atomic weight depends on its origin gave the first chemical proof of isotopes, linking analytical precision to atomic structure.

flashcards.front: What did Richards win the Nobel for?
flashcards.back: Highly accurate determinations of the atomic weights of many elements.

flashcards.front: What did lead from radioactive ores reveal?
flashcards.back: Different atomic weights, chemical evidence for isotopes.

motivation: for his researches on plant pigments, especially chlorophyll
oneLiner: Determined the structure of chlorophyll and other plant pigments.

deepDive.scope: Willstätter won for his researches on plant pigments, above all chlorophyll. He purified chlorophyll, showed it is a defined chemical compound containing magnesium at its core, distinguished chlorophyll a and b, and clarified its relationship to other natural pigments including the blood pigment heme and the flower pigments (anthocyanins) he also studied.
deepDive.history: Plant pigments were poorly understood mixtures. Using new chromatographic-style separation and careful organic analysis in the early 1900s-1910s, Willstätter brought rigorous structural chemistry to these labile natural colorants, foundational for understanding photosynthesis.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Willstätter isolated chlorophyll in pure form and analyzed it, establishing that it is a single class of magnesium-containing compounds built on a porphyrin-like ring system (chlorin), with a long phytol tail. He identified two close forms, chlorophyll a and b.

He recognized the structural kinship between chlorophyll's magnesium-porphyrin core and the iron-porphyrin core of heme (blood pigment), revealing a deep unity in nature's use of metal-chelating tetrapyrrole rings for light capture (Mg) and oxygen transport (Fe).

For flower colors he studied the anthocyanins, showing how a common pigment skeleton gives different colors depending on substitution and pH (acidity), explaining the range of reds, purples, and blues.

His purification and degradation methods, plus careful elemental and functional-group analysis, set the standard for natural-product structure work and prepared the ground for Hans Fischer's later full synthesis of porphyrins (1930).
concepts: Chlorophyll structure: a magnesium-centered porphyrin (chlorin) pigment that captures light.
Pigment kinship: chlorophyll (Mg) and heme (Fe) share a tetrapyrrole ring.
Anthocyanin color: flower pigment color depends on structure and pH.

jargon.definition: The green, magnesium-containing pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
A ring of four linked pyrrole units that can chelate a metal ion.
A class of plant pigments giving red, purple, and blue colors.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Willstätter's structural work on chlorophyll underlies our understanding of photosynthesis, the basis of nearly all life's energy. His insight that chlorophyll and heme share a porphyrin core unified plant and animal biochemistry.

flashcards.front: What metal is at the core of chlorophyll?
flashcards.back: Magnesium.

flashcards.front: What structural feature do chlorophyll and heme share?
flashcards.back: A tetrapyrrole (porphyrin) ring chelating a metal.

motivation: for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements
oneLiner: Synthesized ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, enabling industrial nitrogen fixation.

deepDive.scope: Haber won for the synthesis of ammonia (NH3) directly from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen. Around 1909 he demonstrated a catalytic, high-pressure process combining N2 and H2 over a catalyst, which (scaled up industrially by Carl Bosch at BASF as the Haber-Bosch process) made artificial nitrogen fixation possible at vast scale.
deepDive.history: Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant but inert; fixing it into usable compounds was a grand challenge tied to fertilizer and explosives supply. Haber's process solved a looming food crisis (nitrogen fertilizer) but also enabled wartime explosives. Haber's role in chemical warfare makes him a controversial figure; the Nobel was contentious.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
The reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 is exothermic but extremely slow because the N triple bond in N2 is among the strongest in chemistry, and the equilibrium yield falls as temperature rises. Haber confronted this thermodynamic-kinetic dilemma directly.

Using Le Chatelier's principle, he applied high pressure (which favors the side with fewer gas molecules, the ammonia side) to push equilibrium toward NH3, and a moderately high temperature with an iron-based catalyst (with promoters) to achieve an acceptable rate without destroying yield.

Because single-pass conversion is low, the process recycles unreacted gases and continuously removes ammonia by condensation, shifting equilibrium forward, a marriage of equilibrium thermodynamics and chemical engineering.

The catalyst works by dissociatively adsorbing N2 on the iron surface (the rate-limiting step), allowing nitrogen atoms to combine stepwise with hydrogen, dramatically lowering the activation barrier for breaking the N triple bond.
concepts: Nitrogen fixation: converting inert N2 into reactive compounds like ammonia.
Le Chatelier optimization: high pressure favors ammonia formation.
Heterogeneous catalysis: an iron surface dissociates N2 to speed the reaction.

jargon.definition: Turning unreactive atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds.
A system at equilibrium shifts to counteract an imposed change (e.g., pressure).
An additive that boosts a catalyst's activity or stability.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Haber-Bosch ammonia underlies synthetic fertilizers that feed roughly half the world's population, arguably the most consequential industrial chemical process ever. It also illustrates the dual-use dilemma, as fixed nitrogen serves both food and munitions.

flashcards.back: High pressure shifts equilibrium toward ammonia; the iron catalyst speeds the slow N2 dissociation.

flashcards.front: Why is the Haber process world-changing?
flashcards.back: It enables industrial nitrogen fertilizer feeding much of humanity.

motivation: in recognition of his work in thermochemistry
oneLiner: His heat theorem became the third law of thermodynamics (entropy at absolute zero).

deepDive.scope: Nernst won for his work in thermochemistry, centered on his 1906 heat theorem (the Nernst heat theorem), which developed into the third law of thermodynamics. It concerns how the entropy and free-energy changes of reactions behave as temperature approaches absolute zero, enabling chemical equilibria to be calculated from thermal data.
deepDive.history: Chemists wanted to predict whether and how far reactions proceed (chemical affinity) from measurable heat quantities. Earlier rules (Thomsen-Berthelot) were flawed. Nernst's theorem provided the missing principle, linking thermodynamics to absolute zero and spurring low-temperature physics.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Nernst's heat theorem states that as temperature approaches absolute zero, the entropy change of a reaction between perfectly crystalline solids approaches zero. Equivalently (Planck's later refinement), the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K, the third law.

This matters because the free-energy change DeltaG (which determines reaction direction and equilibrium) relates to the enthalpy change DeltaH and entropy change DeltaS via DeltaG = DeltaH - T DeltaS. Knowing how DeltaS behaves near 0 K lets chemists integrate heat-capacity data up to any temperature and compute equilibrium constants from purely thermal (calorimetric) measurements, no equilibrium experiment needed.

It also implies absolute zero is unattainable in a finite number of steps and that heat capacities vanish as T approaches 0, predictions that drove cryogenic research.

Nernst thus unified thermochemistry with thermodynamics, turning calorimetry into a predictive tool for chemical equilibrium.
concepts: Third law of thermodynamics: entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero at absolute zero.
Free energy and equilibrium: DeltaG = DeltaH - T DeltaS governs reaction spontaneity.
Calorimetric prediction: equilibria computable from heat data via the heat theorem.

jargon.definition: A measure of disorder or the number of microscopic arrangements of a system.
The study of heat changes in chemical reactions.
The lowest possible temperature, 0 K (-273.15 C).

deepDive.whyItMatters: The third law lets chemists predict chemical equilibria from thermal measurements alone and grounds the concept of absolute entropy. It is a pillar of physical chemistry and underpins cryogenics and statistical thermodynamics.

flashcards.front: What did Nernst's heat theorem become?
flashcards.back: The third law of thermodynamics.

flashcards.back: The entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero.

motivation: for his contributions to our knowledge of the chemistry of radioactive substances, and his investigations into the origin and nature of isotopes
oneLiner: Conceived isotopes and the radioactive displacement law of decay.

deepDive.scope: Soddy won for his contributions to radioactive chemistry and especially for the origin and nature of isotopes, a term he coined in 1913. He recognized that some chemically inseparable substances differ in atomic weight and radioactivity, hence are different atomic forms of the same element occupying the same place in the periodic table, and formulated the radioactive displacement laws.
deepDive.history: With Rutherford, Soddy had earlier developed the disintegration theory (1902-1903). The proliferation of dozens of radioactive 'elements' from decay chains overcrowded the periodic table; the concept of isotopes resolved this by showing many were variants of known elements.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Soddy realized that several radioactive products were chemically identical to (and inseparable from) ordinary elements yet had different atomic masses and decay properties. He named these isotopes (Greek: 'same place'), since they share a periodic-table position despite differing in mass.

He formulated the radioactive displacement laws: emitting an alpha particle (helium nucleus) reduces the atomic number by 2 (moving the element two places left in the table) and the mass by 4; emitting a beta particle (electron) raises the atomic number by 1 (one place right) with negligible mass change. This systematized the decay chains.

Together these ideas implied that an element is defined by its nuclear charge (atomic number), not its atomic weight, and that an element can have multiple isotopes of different masses, exactly what Richards's lead measurements (1914) and Aston's mass spectrograph (1922) confirmed.

Soddy thereby distinguished chemical identity (atomic number) from physical mass (isotope), a cornerstone of nuclear chemistry.
concepts: Isotopes: atoms of one element with the same atomic number but different mass.
Radioactive displacement law: alpha emission shifts element 2 places left, beta 1 place right.
Atomic number defines the element: chemical identity depends on nuclear charge, not mass.

jargon.definition: One of several forms of an element differing only in atomic mass (neutron number).
The number of protons in a nucleus, which defines the element.
A rule for how alpha or beta decay changes an atom's position in the periodic table.

deepDive.whyItMatters: The concept of isotopes is fundamental to chemistry, physics, dating, medicine, and nuclear technology. Soddy's displacement laws made sense of radioactive decay series and clarified that elements are defined by atomic number.

flashcards.back: Isotope, atoms of the same element (same place in the table) with different masses.

flashcards.front: State the alpha-decay displacement law.
flashcards.back: Alpha emission lowers atomic number by 2 and mass by 4 (shifts two places left).

flashcards.front: What defines a chemical element?
flashcards.back: Its atomic number (nuclear charge), not its atomic weight.

motivation: for his discovery, by means of his mass spectrograph, of isotopes, in a large number of non-radioactive elements, and for his enunciation of the whole-number rule
oneLiner: Invented the mass spectrograph, found isotopes of stable elements, and the whole-number rule.

deepDive.scope: Aston won for discovering, with his mass spectrograph, that many ordinary (non-radioactive) elements consist of isotopes, and for the whole-number rule: isotopic masses are very nearly whole-number multiples of the hydrogen atom's mass. He measured isotopic masses with high precision and catalogued isotopes across the periodic table.
deepDive.history: Building on J.J. Thomson's positive-ray work, Aston designed (1919) an instrument that sorted ions by mass with unprecedented resolution, revealing that elements like neon are mixtures of isotopes, confirming Soddy's idea for stable elements.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Aston's mass spectrograph ionized atoms and passed the ions through electric and magnetic fields arranged so that ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio focused to the same point regardless of small velocity differences (velocity focusing). The position where each ion landed gave its mass.

This revealed that neon, for instance, is a mixture of mass-20 and mass-22 atoms, explaining its non-integer average atomic weight (about 20.2) as a weighted average of integer-mass isotopes. He extended this to dozens of elements.

He enunciated the whole-number rule: each isotope's mass is close to an integer (in units of hydrogen/oxygen), so atomic weights are non-integer only because elements are mixtures of integer-mass isotopes, vindicating Prout's old hypothesis in modified form.

Aston also measured slight deviations from exact integers (the packing fraction / mass defect), foreshadowing nuclear binding energy and E=mc^2 considerations, the basis of understanding nuclear stability.
concepts: Mass spectrograph: separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio to measure atomic masses.
Whole-number rule: isotopic masses are nearly integers; average atomic weights reflect isotope mixtures.
Mass defect / packing fraction: small deviations from integer mass relate to nuclear binding.

jargon.definition: An instrument that sorts ionized atoms by mass to reveal isotopes.
An ion's mass divided by its charge, the quantity a mass spectrometer measures.
Aston's measure of how much an isotope's mass deviates from a whole number.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Aston's instrument founded mass spectrometry, now indispensable across chemistry, biology, and physics. Cataloguing stable isotopes confirmed nuclear structure, and his mass-defect measurements opened the path to nuclear energy understanding.

flashcards.front: What instrument did Aston invent?
flashcards.back: The mass spectrograph.

flashcards.front: What is the whole-number rule?
flashcards.back: Isotopic masses are nearly whole numbers; non-integer atomic weights come from isotope mixtures.

motivation: for his invention of the method of micro-analysis of organic substances
oneLiner: Invented quantitative organic microanalysis, enabling analysis from milligram samples.

deepDive.scope: Pregl won for inventing quantitative organic microanalysis: methods and apparatus to determine the elemental composition (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, etc.) of organic compounds using only a few milligrams of material, roughly a hundredfold less than classical methods required.
deepDive.history: Studying scarce natural products (like bile acids), Pregl was frustrated that classical combustion analysis needed large samples he could not obtain. From around 1910 he miniaturized the techniques and developed a sensitive microbalance, transforming what analyses were feasible.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Classical elemental analysis burns an organic sample and weighs the CO2 and H2O produced to find carbon and hydrogen content, but it needed hundreds of milligrams. Pregl re-engineered every step for the milligram scale.

Central was a highly sensitive microbalance accurate to about a microgram, letting tiny mass changes be measured reliably. He redesigned combustion trains, absorption tubes, and gas-handling apparatus so that minute quantities of combustion products could be captured and weighed quantitatively.

He developed micro methods for carbon/hydrogen (combustion), nitrogen, halogens, sulfur, and functional-group determinations, all validated for precision at small scale.

By slashing the sample required, Pregl made it possible to characterize rare, precious, or hard-to-isolate substances, accelerating natural-product, biochemical, and pharmaceutical chemistry.
concepts: Microanalysis: quantitative elemental analysis using milligram samples.
Microbalance: a balance precise enough to weigh microgram differences.
Combustion analysis: determining C and H by burning a sample and weighing CO2 and water.

jargon.definition: Chemical analysis carried out on very small (milligram) amounts of material.
An extremely sensitive balance for tiny masses.
Measuring how much of each element a compound contains.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Microanalysis let chemists determine the formulas of scarce natural products and new compounds from tiny samples, indispensable to organic, natural-product, and biochemical research throughout the 20th century.

flashcards.front: What did Pregl invent?
flashcards.back: Quantitative organic microanalysis (elemental analysis from a few milligrams).

flashcards.front: What key instrument enabled microanalysis?
flashcards.back: A highly sensitive microbalance.

motivation: for his demonstration of the heterogenous nature of colloid solutions and for the methods he used, which have since become fundamental in modern colloid chemistry
oneLiner: Proved colloids are heterogeneous and co-invented the ultramicroscope to see them.

deepDive.scope: Zsigmondy won for demonstrating the heterogeneous (particulate) nature of colloidal solutions and for the methods, especially the ultramicroscope he co-developed, that became foundational to colloid chemistry. Working with colloidal gold (gold sols), he showed colloids contain discrete suspended particles rather than being truly homogeneous solutions.
deepDive.history: Colloids (like gold sols, milk, and gels) were puzzling, were they solutions or suspensions? Around 1902 Zsigmondy and Henry Siedentopf built the ultramicroscope, which made individual sub-microscopic particles visible by their scattered light, settling the debate.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Ordinary microscopes cannot resolve colloidal particles (nanometers to fractions of a micron). The ultramicroscope instead illuminates the sample from the side with intense light; each particle scatters light (the Tyndall effect) and appears as a bright point against a dark background, even though it is smaller than the resolution limit.

By counting these flashing points and knowing the concentration, Zsigmondy could estimate particle sizes and numbers, directly proving colloids are heterogeneous dispersions of many tiny particles, not homogeneous like true solutions.

He studied how gold sol particles aggregate and change color (ruby red to blue) with size and coagulation, and how protective colloids stabilize them, foundational concepts of particle stability.

This gave colloid science quantitative, observational tools and underpinned understanding of aerosols, emulsions, gels, and, in modern terms, nanoparticles.
concepts: Colloid heterogeneity: colloidal solutions contain discrete suspended particles.
Ultramicroscope: reveals sub-resolution particles by their scattered light.
Tyndall scattering: colloidal particles scatter light, making beams visible.

jargon.definition: A mixture with particles intermediate in size between dissolved molecules and visible grains, dispersed in a medium.
A colloidal dispersion of solid particles in a liquid (e.g., gold sol).
An instrument that detects tiny particles by the light they scatter.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Zsigmondy founded quantitative colloid chemistry and the methods to observe nanoscale particles, important to materials science, nanotechnology, biology, and industry (paints, inks, foods). His gold-sol work prefigures modern nanoparticle science.

flashcards.front: What did Zsigmondy prove about colloids?
flashcards.back: They are heterogeneous, made of discrete suspended particles.

flashcards.back: The ultramicroscope, which sees particles by their scattered light.

motivation: for his work on disperse systems
oneLiner: Invented the ultracentrifuge to measure particle and macromolecule sizes in disperse systems.

deepDive.scope: Theodor (The) Svedberg won for his work on disperse systems (colloids), centered on his invention of the analytical ultracentrifuge. This spun samples at enormous speeds to sediment colloidal particles and macromolecules, allowing precise determination of their size, mass, and uniformity.
deepDive.history: Building on colloid chemistry (cf. Zsigmondy), Svedberg sought to characterize particle sizes quantitatively. In the 1920s he developed centrifuges generating up to hundreds of thousands of times gravity, enabling sedimentation of even dissolved proteins.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
In a strong centrifugal field, particles sediment at a rate determined by their mass, size, shape, and the medium's density and viscosity. Svedberg measured sedimentation velocity optically as a moving boundary, deriving the sedimentation coefficient (now expressed in svedberg units, S).

From sedimentation and diffusion data he calculated particle molecular weights via the Svedberg equation, and from the sharpness of the sedimenting boundary he judged whether a sample was uniform (monodisperse) or a mixture.

A landmark finding was that proteins like hemoglobin sediment as discrete, uniform particles of definite molecular weight, evidence that proteins are true, well-defined macromolecules rather than ill-defined aggregates, a pivotal result for biochemistry.

The ultracentrifuge thus turned colloid and macromolecular chemistry into a precise, quantitative science.
concepts: Ultracentrifugation: using extreme centrifugal force to sediment small particles and macromolecules.
Sedimentation coefficient: a measure (in svedbergs) of how fast a particle sediments.
Macromolecule definition: proteins are discrete molecules of definite mass.

jargon.definition: A very high-speed centrifuge used to sediment tiny particles and large molecules.
A mixture of particles dispersed throughout a medium (a colloid).
The unit of sedimentation rate, named after Svedberg.

deepDive.whyItMatters: The ultracentrifuge became essential for determining the size and purity of proteins, nucleic acids, and viruses, foundational to molecular biology (ribosome subunits are still named by their S values) and to colloid and polymer science.

flashcards.back: The analytical ultracentrifuge.

flashcards.back: They are discrete macromolecules of definite molecular weight.

motivation: for his investigations of the constitution of the bile acids and related substances
oneLiner: Determined the structures of the bile acids, key to the steroid skeleton.

deepDive.scope: Wieland won for elucidating the constitution (chemical structure) of the bile acids, such as cholic acid, and related substances. His painstaking degradation studies established their molecular framework and revealed their relationship to cholesterol, helping define the steroid ring system.
deepDive.history: Bile acids, steroid compounds from bile, had complex, unknown structures. From the 1910s-1920s Wieland systematically degraded them chemically. His work, together with Windaus's on sterols (1928 Nobel), built the foundation of steroid chemistry (the precise ring structure was finalized soon after, with some early formulas later corrected).
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Wieland used controlled chemical degradation, oxidation and stepwise breakdown, to fragment bile acid molecules into identifiable smaller pieces, then reasoned backward to the parent structure. By relating bile acids to one another and to cholesterol through chemical transformations, he showed they share a common multi-ring carbon skeleton.

He established that bile acids are built on the steroid nucleus, a fused system of (as later precisely defined) three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, with a carboxylic-acid-bearing side chain. This connected bile acids biochemically to cholesterol as their precursor.

He also contributed to understanding biological oxidation, proposing that oxidation in living systems often proceeds by removal of hydrogen (dehydrogenation) rather than direct oxygen addition, an important mechanistic insight.

The structural work was so intricate that the exact ring arrangement was refined shortly afterward (via X-ray data), but Wieland's framework was decisive.
concepts: Bile acid structure: steroid-based acids derived from cholesterol.
Chemical degradation: breaking a molecule into known fragments to deduce its structure.
Biological oxidation as dehydrogenation: oxidation by removing hydrogen.

jargon.definition: A steroid acid made in the liver from cholesterol that aids fat digestion.
The characteristic four-fused-ring carbon skeleton of steroids.
Systematically breaking a molecule down to identify its parts.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Wieland's bile-acid work helped establish the steroid skeleton common to cholesterol, hormones, and vitamins, central to physiology, pharmacology, and medicine. His dehydrogenation view shaped understanding of metabolism.

flashcards.front: What structures did Wieland elucidate?
flashcards.back: The bile acids (e.g., cholic acid) and their relation to cholesterol.

flashcards.front: What is the steroid nucleus?
flashcards.back: A fused four-ring carbon skeleton shared by steroids.

motivation: for the services rendered through his research into the constitution of the sterols and their connection with the vitamins
oneLiner: Elucidated sterol structures and linked them to vitamin D.

deepDive.scope: Windaus won for research on the constitution of the sterols (especially cholesterol and ergosterol) and their connection with the vitamins, notably the discovery that vitamin D forms from a sterol (ergosterol) by irradiation with ultraviolet light. His work tied steroid structural chemistry to nutrition and the cure of rickets.
deepDive.history: Cholesterol's structure was a major unsolved problem; Windaus, alongside Wieland, worked it out (with the precise ring connectivity finalized around 1932 after X-ray input). Crucially, he discovered the chemical origin of the antirachitic (anti-rickets) vitamin D.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Windaus determined the structure of cholesterol and related sterols through extensive chemical degradation and synthesis, showing they share the steroid four-ring nucleus with a hydroxyl group and a side chain. His and Wieland's structures were close, and X-ray crystallography soon corrected a detail of the ring fusion.

His landmark biochemical insight: the sterol ergosterol, when irradiated with ultraviolet light, is converted into vitamin D (an antirachitic compound). The UV light breaks one of the sterol's rings (a photochemical ring-opening), transforming an inactive sterol into the active vitamin.

This explained why sunlight (UV) prevents and cures rickets: it photochemically generates vitamin D in skin from a sterol precursor, linking molecular structure, photochemistry, and physiology.

Thus Windaus connected the abstract steroid skeleton to a concrete vitamin and a public-health disease, a powerful demonstration of structural biochemistry's relevance.
concepts: Sterol structure: cholesterol and ergosterol are steroid alcohols.
Photochemical vitamin D formation: UV light converts ergosterol to vitamin D.
Structure-function link: a sterol's transformation produces a physiologically active vitamin.

jargon.definition: A steroid bearing a hydroxyl group, such as cholesterol.
A sterol that, on UV irradiation, becomes vitamin D.
Acting against rickets (the role of vitamin D).

deepDive.whyItMatters: Windaus established sterol structures fundamental to biochemistry and revealed how vitamin D arises, underpinning prevention of rickets and modern understanding of vitamin D physiology and the steroid family.

flashcards.back: Sterols (like cholesterol) and their link to vitamins.
