flashcards.back: UV irradiation converts ergosterol into vitamin D.

laureates: Hans Karl August Simon von Euler-Chelpin
motivation: for their investigations on the fermentation of sugar and fermentative enzymes
oneLiner: Revealed the enzymes and coenzymes (and phosphate steps) of sugar fermentation.

deepDive.scope: Harden and von Euler-Chelpin shared the prize for investigations on the fermentation of sugar and fermentative enzymes. They showed that alcoholic fermentation requires not only protein enzymes but also small, heat-stable cofactors (coenzymes), and that inorganic phosphate is consumed, becoming incorporated into sugar phosphate intermediates, early glimpses of the glycolytic pathway.
deepDive.history: After Buchner proved cell-free fermentation (1907), the detailed machinery remained unknown. Harden discovered (around 1905-1906) that dialyzing yeast juice stopped fermentation unless a small dialyzable factor was added back, revealing the coenzyme. Euler-Chelpin later characterized this cofactor (cozymase, now known as NAD).
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Harden found that yeast extract loses fermenting power when dialyzed (which removes small molecules), but activity is restored by adding back the boiled, dialyzed filtrate. This proved fermentation needs two components: a heat-labile enzyme (protein) and a heat-stable, low-molecular-weight coenzyme.

He also discovered that fermentation consumes inorganic phosphate, which becomes esterified to sugar, isolating a sugar diphosphate (the Harden-Young ester, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate). This was the first evidence that phosphorylated sugars are obligatory intermediates in carbohydrate breakdown, a cornerstone of metabolic biochemistry.

Euler-Chelpin elucidated the chemical nature and role of the coenzyme (cozymase / NAD), showing how it participates as a hydrogen/electron carrier in the fermentation reactions.

Together they transformed fermentation from a single mysterious process into a defined sequence of enzyme-catalyzed steps involving coenzymes and phosphorylated intermediates, the conceptual seed of glycolysis.
concepts: Coenzyme requirement: enzymes often need small heat-stable cofactors (e.g., NAD).
Sugar phosphorylation: phosphate is incorporated into sugar intermediates during fermentation.
Pathway thinking: fermentation is a multi-step enzymatic sequence.

jargon.definition: A small non-protein molecule an enzyme needs to function.
The old name for the fermentation coenzyme now known as NAD.
Attaching a phosphate group to a molecule.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Discovering coenzymes and phosphorylated sugar intermediates launched the study of metabolic pathways and bioenergetics. NAD and sugar phosphates are central to glycolysis and cellular energy metabolism in all life.

flashcards.front: What two components did Harden show fermentation needs?
flashcards.back: A heat-labile enzyme and a heat-stable coenzyme (cozymase/NAD).

flashcards.front: What did the consumption of phosphate reveal?
flashcards.back: Sugar phosphate intermediates (e.g., fructose-1,6-bisphosphate) in fermentation.

motivation: for his researches into the constitution of haemin and chlorophyll and especially for his synthesis of haemin
oneLiner: Determined and synthesized haemin, the iron-porphyrin of blood, and studied chlorophyll.

deepDive.scope: Hans Fischer won for elucidating the structures of haemin (the iron-containing red pigment of blood, related to hemoglobin's heme) and chlorophyll, and especially for accomplishing the total synthesis of haemin. He established the detailed porphyrin architecture of these vital pigments.
deepDive.history: Building on Willstätter's pigment work (1915), Fischer attacked the precise constitution of the porphyrin pigments through the 1920s. His 1929 synthesis of haemin was a tour de force confirming the structure of the blood pigment, and he continued toward chlorophyll and bile pigments.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Heme/haemin is built on a porphyrin: four pyrrole rings joined into a large macrocycle that chelates a central metal ion, iron in heme (giving blood its color and oxygen-binding ability), magnesium in chlorophyll.

Fischer determined exactly how the four pyrroles are linked and which side chains (methyl, vinyl, propionic acid groups) occupy which positions around the ring, distinguishing among many possible isomers. He systematized porphyrins by numbering and naming the substitution patterns.

His crowning achievement was synthesizing haemin from simpler pyrrole-derived building blocks, assembling the macrocycle and inserting iron, thereby proving the proposed structure by construction, the gold standard of structural chemistry.

He extended this understanding to chlorophyll and to the bile pigments (breakdown products of heme), revealing a unified family of biologically crucial tetrapyrrole molecules underlying respiration, photosynthesis, and pigment metabolism.
concepts: Porphyrin macrocycle: four pyrroles forming a metal-chelating ring.
Heme vs chlorophyll: iron-porphyrin for oxygen transport vs magnesium-porphyrin for light capture.
Synthesis as proof: total synthesis confirms a proposed structure.

jargon.definition: A crystalline iron-porphyrin derivative of the blood pigment heme.
A macrocycle of four pyrrole rings that binds a central metal.
A five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, the building block of porphyrins.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Fischer's synthesis and structural work defined the porphyrin pigments essential to oxygen transport (heme) and photosynthesis (chlorophyll), foundational to biochemistry, hematology, and the chemistry of life's pigments.

flashcards.front: What did Hans Fischer synthesize?
flashcards.back: Haemin, the iron-porphyrin of the blood pigment.

flashcards.front: What ring system underlies heme and chlorophyll?
flashcards.back: The porphyrin (tetrapyrrole) macrocycle.

motivation: in recognition of their contributions to the invention and development of chemical high pressure methods
oneLiner: Developed industrial high-pressure chemistry: ammonia (Bosch) and coal liquefaction (Bergius).

deepDive.scope: Bosch and Bergius shared the prize for inventing and developing chemical high-pressure methods. Bosch engineered the industrial-scale Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis (turning Haber's lab process into a working factory technology), and Bergius developed high-pressure hydrogenation of coal into liquid fuels (the Bergius process).
deepDive.history: Running reactions at high pressure and temperature on a large scale demanded new chemical engineering, pressure-resistant reactors, durable catalysts, and continuous gas handling. Bosch solved these for ammonia in the 1910s; Bergius applied high-pressure hydrogenation to coal in the same era. This was the first chemistry Nobel emphasizing chemical engineering.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
High pressure shifts equilibria toward products that occupy less volume (Le Chatelier) and increases reactant concentrations, boosting rates, making it powerful for gas-phase syntheses like ammonia and hydrogenation.

Bosch's challenge was practical: at the high pressures and hydrogen temperatures needed for ammonia, ordinary steel was attacked by hydrogen (embrittlement and decarburization). He devised lined reactors, robust catalysts and purification trains, and continuous-flow plant design, enabling tonnage ammonia production.

Bergius hydrogenated coal: by reacting powdered coal with hydrogen at high pressure and temperature (with catalysts), he broke the large carbon-rich coal molecules and added hydrogen to yield liquid hydrocarbons, synthetic oil and gasoline, a route to liquid fuel from coal.

Both processes show how thermodynamic favorability under pressure, combined with catalysis and engineering, converts simple feedstocks (air, coal, hydrogen) into essential products at industrial scale.
concepts: High-pressure synthesis: pressure shifts equilibria and speeds gas reactions.
Chemical engineering of catalysis: reactor design and materials make lab reactions industrial.
Coal hydrogenation: adding hydrogen under pressure converts coal to liquid fuels.

jargon.definition: The industrial high-pressure catalytic synthesis of ammonia.
Adding hydrogen to a substance, here to convert coal into liquids.
Weakening of steel by hydrogen at high pressure/temperature, a key engineering hurdle.

deepDive.whyItMatters: High-pressure methods enabled mass production of fertilizer (ammonia) and synthetic fuels, transforming agriculture, energy, and the chemical industry, and establishing chemical engineering as central to applied chemistry.

flashcards.front: What did Bosch contribute?
flashcards.back: Industrial-scale engineering of high-pressure ammonia synthesis (Haber-Bosch).

flashcards.front: What did Bergius develop?
flashcards.back: High-pressure hydrogenation of coal into liquid fuels.

motivation: for his discoveries and investigations in surface chemistry
oneLiner: Founded modern surface chemistry: monolayer adsorption and the Langmuir isotherm.

deepDive.scope: Langmuir won for his discoveries and investigations in surface chemistry. He established that adsorption on surfaces often forms a single molecular layer (monolayer), formulated the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, and clarified the structure and behavior of surface films and adsorbed layers, founding surface science.
deepDive.history: Working at General Electric (initially on light bulbs and gas-filled lamps), Langmuir studied how gases interact with hot filaments and surfaces. From around 1916 he developed a rigorous, atomistic picture of surfaces, complemented by his and Katharine Blodgett's work on molecular films on liquids.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Langmuir argued that a solid (or liquid) surface presents a fixed array of sites, and that adsorbed molecules bind to these sites, typically forming at most one molecule-thick layer (a monolayer), because surface forces are short-range.

From this he derived the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, relating surface coverage to gas pressure: coverage rises with pressure and saturates as all sites fill. The model assumes equivalent, independent sites and a balance between adsorption and desorption rates, a kinetic-equilibrium treatment.

This monolayer concept explained heterogeneous catalysis, reactant molecules adsorb onto catalyst surface sites where they react, and the behavior of films on liquids (he and Blodgett built ordered molecular monolayers, Langmuir-Blodgett films).

Langmuir also contributed to bonding ideas (extending the Lewis octet, electron sharing) and plasma physics, but the Nobel centered on his quantitative, mechanistic surface chemistry.
concepts: Monolayer adsorption: molecules typically adsorb as a single layer on a surface.
Langmuir isotherm: surface coverage versus pressure saturates as sites fill.
Surface catalysis: reactions occur on adsorbed surface sites.

jargon.definition: The sticking of molecules onto a surface (distinct from absorption into a bulk).
A single-molecule-thick layer on a surface.
A relationship measured at constant temperature, here coverage versus pressure.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Langmuir's surface chemistry underpins heterogeneous catalysis (most industrial chemistry), adsorption technologies, thin-film science, and surface analysis. The Langmuir isotherm remains a standard model, and Langmuir-Blodgett films seeded nanoscience.

flashcards.front: What field did Langmuir found?
flashcards.back: Modern surface chemistry.

flashcards.front: What does the Langmuir isotherm describe?
flashcards.back: How surface coverage by adsorbed molecules depends on pressure, saturating at a monolayer.

motivation: for his discovery of heavy hydrogen
oneLiner: Discovered deuterium (heavy hydrogen), the mass-2 isotope of hydrogen.

deepDive.scope: Urey won for discovering heavy hydrogen, the hydrogen isotope of mass 2 (deuterium), which he detected spectroscopically in 1931 and then concentrated. He also pioneered methods to separate isotopes and showed how isotopic substitution affects molecular properties.
deepDive.history: By 1931 isotopes of many elements were known, but hydrogen, the lightest element, was thought to be essentially a single species. Predicting a rare heavy isotope, Urey designed an experiment to find it, opening the chemistry of isotopes and isotope effects.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Urey reasoned that if a mass-2 hydrogen isotope existed, it would have very slightly different atomic spectral lines than ordinary mass-1 hydrogen because the heavier nucleus shifts energy levels (the reduced-mass effect). The isotope's natural abundance is tiny (about 1 in 6500), so the lines would be faint.

To enhance them, he evaporated a large quantity of liquid hydrogen down to a small residue, concentrating the less-volatile heavy isotope, then examined the atomic emission spectrum. He observed faint new lines at exactly the wavelengths predicted for mass-2 hydrogen, confirming deuterium.

He and others then separated deuterium in bulk, notably as heavy water (D2O), exploiting small differences in physical and electrochemical behavior between H and D (a large isotope effect because deuterium is twice the mass of protium).

Because deuterium differs so much in relative mass, it produces pronounced kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects, making it an invaluable tracer and mechanistic probe, and heavy water became important in nuclear reactors as a neutron moderator.
concepts: Deuterium: the hydrogen isotope with a proton and a neutron (mass 2).
Spectroscopic isotope detection: isotopes shift spectral lines via nuclear mass.
Isotope separation by distillation/electrolysis: concentrating a rare heavy isotope.

jargon.definition: Heavy hydrogen, an isotope with one proton and one neutron.
Water made with deuterium (D2O) instead of ordinary hydrogen.
A change in reaction rate or properties when an atom is replaced by a heavier isotope.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Deuterium and heavy water are essential tools: deuterium labeling probes reaction mechanisms and is used in NMR and tracer studies, while heavy water moderates neutrons in nuclear reactors. The discovery extended isotope chemistry to hydrogen and revealed large isotope effects.

flashcards.front: What did Urey discover?
flashcards.back: Deuterium, the mass-2 (heavy) isotope of hydrogen.

flashcards.front: How did he first detect it?
flashcards.back: By faint predicted spectral lines after concentrating heavy hydrogen from evaporated liquid hydrogen.

flashcards.front: What is heavy water?
flashcards.back: Water made with deuterium, D2O, used as a neutron moderator.

motivation: in recognition of their synthesis of new radioactive elements
oneLiner: Created artificial radioactivity, synthesizing new radioactive isotopes by bombardment.

deepDive.scope: Frederic Joliot and Irene Joliot-Curie shared the prize for the synthesis of new radioactive elements, the discovery of artificial (induced) radioactivity in 1934. By bombarding light elements with alpha particles, they produced new, previously nonexistent radioactive isotopes, showing that radioactivity could be created at will, not just found in nature.
deepDive.history: Irene was the daughter of Marie and Pierre Curie, continuing the family's radioactivity research. In 1934, irradiating aluminium and other light elements with alpha particles from polonium, the couple noticed the targets remained radioactive after the source was removed, proof of newly created radioactive nuclei.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
They bombarded light targets (such as aluminium, boron, magnesium) with alpha particles. An alpha particle (helium nucleus) can fuse with a target nucleus, ejecting a neutron and forming a new, heavier nucleus, for example, aluminium-27 + alpha yields phosphorus-30 + a neutron.

The product phosphorus-30 is an artificial radioactive isotope not found in nature: it decays (by positron emission) with its own characteristic half-life. Crucially, the irradiated sample kept emitting radiation after the alpha source was withdrawn, decaying exponentially, unmistakable evidence of a genuine new radioactive species.

They confirmed the products chemically: by dissolving and separating the irradiated material, they showed the radioactivity belonged to a different element than the target (e.g., phosphorus, then nitrogen/silicon daughters), proving transmutation had created a new radioelement.

This demonstrated that nuclear reactions can synthesize radioactive isotopes of ordinary elements, generalizing Rutherford's transmutation and Soddy's isotopes to deliberate creation, and immediately enabled radioactive tracers for science and medicine.
concepts: Artificial radioactivity: bombardment can create radioactive isotopes not found in nature.
Alpha-induced transmutation: an alpha particle fuses with a nucleus, ejecting a neutron and forming a new element.
Chemical identification of radioelements: separating the new active species proves the element changed.

jargon.definition: Radioactivity created by bombarding stable nuclei with particles.
Striking target nuclei with alpha particles to induce nuclear reactions.
A radioactive isotope of an element.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Artificial radioactivity made radioisotopes available on demand, revolutionizing medicine (diagnosis and therapy), biology (tracers), and research, and was a key step toward nuclear fission and the broader exploitation of nuclear reactions.

flashcards.front: What did the Joliot-Curies discover in 1934?
flashcards.back: Artificial (induced) radioactivity, creating new radioactive isotopes by bombardment.

flashcards.front: Give an example of their nuclear reaction.
flashcards.back: Aluminium-27 + alpha -> phosphorus-30 (radioactive) + a neutron.

flashcards.front: Why was the effect convincing?
flashcards.back: Targets kept emitting radiation, decaying with a characteristic half-life, after the source was removed.

motivation: for his contributions to our knowledge of molecular structure through his investigations on dipole moments and on the diffraction of X-rays and electrons in gases
oneLiner: Probed molecular structure via dipole moments and X-ray/electron diffraction.

deepDive.scope: Debye won for contributions to knowledge of molecular structure through his work on dipole moments and on the diffraction of X-rays and electrons by gases. He showed how measuring a molecule's dipole moment and its diffraction pattern reveals charge distribution, shape, and bond geometry.
deepDive.history: In the 1910s-1930s, determining molecular shapes and polarity was a frontier. Debye, a physicist-chemist, developed quantitative theories connecting macroscopic measurements (dielectric behavior, scattering) to molecular structure, and the dipole-moment unit (the debye) bears his name.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
A polar molecule has a permanent dipole moment because its positive and negative charge centers do not coincide (e.g., water). Debye showed that a substance's dielectric constant and its temperature dependence reveal the molecular dipole moment, via the Debye equation relating polarization to permanent dipoles plus induced polarizability. From the dipole moment one infers bond polarity and molecular geometry (a symmetric molecule like CO2 has zero net dipole; a bent one like water does not).

For diffraction, Debye (with Scherrer) developed powder X-ray diffraction and, importantly, the theory of X-ray and electron scattering by gas-phase molecules. The scattered intensity pattern encodes interatomic distances; analyzing it yields bond lengths and angles of free molecules, not just crystals.

Electron diffraction in gases became a primary method for determining the structures of small molecules, complementing X-ray crystallography for solids.

Thus Debye provided both a polarity probe (dipole moments) and geometry probes (diffraction), turning physical measurements into structural information, foundational physical chemistry.
concepts: Dipole moment: a measure of a molecule's charge separation/polarity.
Dielectric method: dielectric constant vs temperature yields the dipole moment.
Gas-phase diffraction: scattering of X-rays/electrons reveals bond lengths and angles.

jargon.definition: A vector measuring how separated a molecule's positive and negative charge are.
The unit of molecular dipole moment, named after Debye.
Scattering of electrons used to determine molecular geometry.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Debye's methods are core physical-chemistry tools: dipole moments characterize polarity and bonding, and X-ray/electron diffraction determine molecular and crystal structures, underpinning chemistry, materials science, and structural biology.

flashcards.front: What two kinds of measurement did Debye use to probe structure?
flashcards.back: Dipole moments and X-ray/electron diffraction.

flashcards.front: What does a molecule's dipole moment indicate?
flashcards.back: Its charge separation/polarity, hence bond polarity and shape.

motivation: Walter Norman Haworth "for his investigations on carbohydrates and vitamin C"; Paul Karrer "for his investigations on carotenoids, flavins and vitamins A and B2"
oneLiner: Structures of carbohydrates and vitamin C (Haworth) and of carotenoids/vitamins A, B2 (Karrer).

deepDive.scope: The 1937 prize was shared. Haworth won for work on carbohydrates and vitamin C, he determined the ring structures of sugars (the Haworth projection) and the structure of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), achieving its synthesis, the first vitamin to be synthesized. Karrer won for elucidating the structures of carotenoids, flavins, and vitamins A and B2 (riboflavin).
deepDive.history: The 1920s-30s were the golden age of vitamin chemistry. Building on Fischer's sugar work, Haworth clarified sugar ring forms; his vitamin C synthesis (with Reichstein independently) was a milestone. Karrer's structural work on carotene and vitamin A linked plant pigments to nutrition.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Haworth showed that sugars in solution exist mainly as rings (pyranose six-membered or furanose five-membered), not open chains, and devised the Haworth projection to depict these rings in three dimensions, clarifying anomeric configuration and glycosidic linkages, the basis of carbohydrate structure.

He determined that vitamin C is ascorbic acid, a relatively simple sugar-derived lactone, and synthesized it, proving the structure and enabling industrial production of the antiscorbutic vitamin.

Karrer elucidated the carotenoids (e.g., beta-carotene), long-chain polyene pigments, and showed that beta-carotene is a provitamin: the body cleaves it to form vitamin A (retinol). He established vitamin A's structure and that of riboflavin (vitamin B2) and the flavins, relating molecular structure to nutritional function.

Together their work connected the structures of sugars, vitamins, and pigments to biology, and demonstrated that vitamins are definite chemical compounds that can be synthesized.
concepts: Sugar ring forms: sugars predominantly cyclize into pyranose/furanose rings (Haworth projection).
Vitamin C as ascorbic acid: a synthesizable, defined molecule.
Provitamin conversion: beta-carotene is cleaved to vitamin A.

jargon.definition: A standard way of drawing the ring form of a sugar.
A class of yellow-orange polyene plant pigments (e.g., beta-carotene).
A precursor the body converts into a vitamin.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Haworth's carbohydrate ring chemistry and the synthesis of vitamin C transformed nutrition and industry, while Karrer's structures of carotenoids and vitamins A and B2 underpinned vitamin science and the understanding of dietary pigments.

flashcards.front: What is the Haworth projection used for?
flashcards.back: Depicting the ring (cyclic) structures of sugars.

flashcards.front: What did Karrer show about beta-carotene?
flashcards.back: It is a provitamin cleaved by the body to form vitamin A.

motivation: for his work on carotenoids and vitamins
oneLiner: Elucidated carotenoid pigments and vitamins (riboflavin and vitamin B6).

deepDive.scope: Kuhn won for his work on carotenoids and vitamins. He isolated and determined the structures of numerous carotenoid pigments and contributed key structural work on vitamins, including riboflavin (vitamin B2) and the isolation/characterization of vitamin B6, advancing the chemistry of these biologically essential molecules.
deepDive.history: Working in the same vitamin/pigment era as Karrer (with whom he sometimes competed), Kuhn applied advanced separation and microanalytical methods to isolate pure carotenoids and vitamins from natural sources in the 1930s. He was awarded the prize in 1938 but, under Nazi-era pressure, was compelled to decline it at the time and received the diploma/medal after the war.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Carotenoids are long conjugated polyene chains; their extended alternating double bonds (conjugation) absorb visible light, giving their colors, and make them sensitive to handling. Kuhn used careful chromatographic separation to isolate individual carotenoids from complex mixtures and determined how many double bonds and what end groups each contained, refining the relationship between conjugation length and color.

For vitamins, he established the structure of riboflavin (vitamin B2), part of the flavin coenzymes, and isolated vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), characterizing its structure. These required isolating tiny amounts of pure substance and deducing structure by degradation and synthesis.

His work tied the precise molecular architecture of pigments and vitamins to their biological roles (as coenzymes and nutrients), reinforcing that vitamins are definite, synthesizable compounds.

Kuhn also advanced understanding of conjugated systems and stereochemistry of polyenes, relevant to color and reactivity.
concepts: Conjugated polyenes: alternating double bonds give carotenoids their color.
Vitamin structure determination: isolating and characterizing B2 and B6.
Coenzyme role: flavins (from riboflavin) act as biological cofactors.

jargon.definition: A conjugated polyene plant/animal pigment, often yellow-orange.
Vitamin B2, a precursor of flavin coenzymes.
Alternating single and double bonds that delocalize electrons and absorb light.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Kuhn's structural chemistry of carotenoids and vitamins advanced nutrition, coenzyme biochemistry, and the chemistry of conjugated pigments. His isolation of vitamin B6 and work on B2 were important for understanding essential nutrients.

flashcards.front: What did Kuhn win the Nobel for?
flashcards.back: His work on carotenoids and vitamins.

flashcards.front: Which vitamins are associated with Kuhn's work?
flashcards.back: Riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B6.

motivation: Adolf Butenandt "for his work on sex hormones"; Leopold Ruzicka "for his work on polymethylenes and higher terpenes"
oneLiner: Sex hormone structures (Butenandt) and large-ring terpene chemistry (Ruzicka).

deepDive.scope: The 1939 prize was shared. Butenandt won for work on the sex hormones, he isolated and determined the structures of estrone, androsterone, and progesterone, key steroid hormones. Ruzicka won for work on polymethylenes (large carbon rings) and higher terpenes, including establishing the structures of musk macrocyclic compounds and developing the isoprene rule of terpene biosynthesis. Butenandt, like Kuhn, was forced by the Nazi regime to decline initially and received the award after the war.
deepDive.history: In the early 1930s sex hormones were isolated in tiny quantities from enormous amounts of biological material; Butenandt's structural work built on the steroid chemistry of Wieland and Windaus. Ruzicka overturned the belief that only small carbon rings were stable by synthesizing large-ring musk compounds, and systematized terpene chemistry begun by Wallach.
deepDive.chemistryLogic:
Butenandt isolated estrone (from urine) and androsterone, then determined that the sex hormones are steroids, built on the same four-ring nucleus as cholesterol and bile acids, differing in oxidation pattern and side groups. Establishing these structures (and later partial syntheses) revealed how subtle changes to the steroid skeleton produce distinct hormonal activities (estrogenic vs androgenic vs progestational).

Ruzicka demonstrated that stable carbon rings can be very large (up to many-membered macrocycles), explaining the structures of natural musks like muscone and civetone as large-ring ketones, contradicting the prevailing view that only 5- and 6-membered rings were favorable.

For terpenes, he advanced the isoprene rule: terpenes and related natural products are assembled from isoprene (C5) units in regular head-to-tail patterns, and he extended this to higher terpenes and to the biosynthetic relationship between terpenes and steroids.

Together their work deepened steroid and terpenoid chemistry, classes that include hormones, fragrances, vitamins, and many drugs, linking molecular architecture to biological and sensory function.
concepts: Steroid hormones: sex hormones are steroids on the four-ring nucleus.
Large carbon rings: macrocyclic compounds (musks) are stable and natural.
Isoprene rule: terpenes are built from C5 isoprene units.

jargon.definition: A steroid (e.g., estrone, testosterone, progesterone) regulating reproductive function.
A large ring molecule with many atoms in the ring.
The principle that terpenes are assembled from five-carbon isoprene units.

deepDive.whyItMatters: Butenandt's hormone structures founded steroid endocrinology and pharmacology (including later contraceptives and corticosteroids). Ruzicka's macrocycle and isoprene-rule work shaped fragrance chemistry and the understanding of terpenoid and steroid biosynthesis.

flashcards.front: What did Butenandt determine?
flashcards.back: The structures of sex hormones (estrone, androsterone, progesterone) as steroids.

flashcards.front: What is the isoprene rule (Ruzicka)?
flashcards.back: Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units.

oneLiner: No prize awarded this year.
